Scholarly estimates for the total population of the Roman Empire at its height vary considerably, reflecting genuine disagreement among researchers. [d2] (Wikipedia, citing historian Kyle Harper) places the empire's population at between 59 and 76 million in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE, with Harper's own estimate at 75 million at its peak. [d3] (Wikipedia's Roman Empire article) notes that recent demographic studies have argued for a population peak ranging from 70 million to more than 100 million. [d10] gives a narrower modern scholarly range of approximately 55 to 70 million, while [d6] estimates 50 to 90 million — roughly 20% of the world's population at the time — and [d4] suggests estimates vary from as low as 50 million to as high as 100 million, with 70 million as the most likely figure. [d8] cites Kyle Harper's figure of 60 million during the reign of Augustus (27 BCE–14 CE), growing at 0.1% annually. It is worth noting that some sources (d1, d5, d7, d9) cite a figure of approximately 1 million, but this refers specifically to the city of Rome, not the empire as a whole, as confirmed by [d2] and [d9] (Britannica). In sum, while there is no consensus, the most commonly cited scholarly range for the entire Roman Empire's population at its height falls roughly between 55 and 100 million people.
